source: Lovett & Anderson (1995) Making heads or tails out of how people select problem-solving strategies (CogSci 17; precursor of the 1996 Cognitive Psychology paper)
finding: Building Sticks Task with experimenter-set success rates for the two strategies. People mostly chose the more successful strategy and often overmatched. An ACT-R model that treats each strategy's chance of success as a Bayesian posterior over past successes and failures, plus Gaussian noise, fit well in aggregate and less well for single people.
numbers: N=68 CMU undergraduates (one removed, 67 analysed); 90 problems each; 4 conditions: complementary high 80/20, complementary low 60/40, non-complementary high and low. Matching-law predictions about 0.94 (noncomp-hi) and 0.69 (noncomp-lo); observed close. Over 80% choice of better strategy in comp-hi. Extreme preferrers (at least 43 of last 45 problems): 3/17 comp-hi (18%), 2/15 noncomp-lo (13%), 1/17 comp-lo (6%). Matching law fit to individuals R2=.60. ACT-R model: noise variance 0.052, one free parameter (alpha+beta fit to 255), R2=.99 over all subject-problem pairs, R2=.66 for individuals' last 45 problems.
limits: Read through a page summary only (the 1996 journal paper was not reachable). The page does not report how many people stuck with overshoot; it says which strategy was the better one did not change results. Individual fit is weak (R2=.66): learning rate and exploration value differ across people. Prior strength is fitted, not fixed.
agent_relevance: A concrete human-data anchor for success-count based operator choice: Beta-style posterior, small Gaussian noise (SD about 0.23), prior strength in the hundreds. People overmatch, so a greedy-leaning softmax (low temperature) is closer to humans than pure probability matching.

source: Xie & Moss (2025) Task representation and individual differences affect strategy selection and problem-solving performance (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: A replication of Lovett and Schunn (1999) on the Building Sticks Task found the four predictions held: people shift toward the strategy that works and down-weight a cue that stops being predictive. The paper does not test Lovett and Anderson (1996) itself.
numbers: 144 recruited, 100 analysed (about 25 per cell); 2x2 design: cue predictive 80/20 vs unpredictive 50/50 by base-rate bias 70/30 vs 50/50; 80 training problems with pretest and posttest. Posttest: biased group chose successful strategy more (b=0.46, p=0.009). Cue slope in unpredictive-biased stayed positive (b=0.49, p<0.001), so down-weighting is gradual. Length-based strategy reports 45% vs 69% (chi2=10.79, p=0.001). Attentional control (b=-0.06, p<0.01) and inductive reasoning (b=-0.05, p<0.01) predicted faster solutions; working memory capacity did not (b=0.01, p=0.83). Power analysis used partial eta2=0.35 from Lovett and Schunn.
limits: Only the first 100,000 of 123,767 characters were read. Authors say results are also compatible with rational metareasoning, without discrete representation change. Individual-difference results exploratory. Not a replication of the utility equation as such.
agent_relevance: A different lab confirms that humans learn operator preference from experienced success and drop a cue slowly, not at once. Supports slow, count-based updating. Gives a competing account (metareasoning) that predicts the same behaviour.

source: Fu & Anderson (2004) Extending the computational abilities of the procedural learning mechanism in ACT-R (CogSci 26)
finding: The original ACT-R utility learning only handles yes/no feedback. A temporal-difference version, where reward is passed back to earlier productions with hyperbolic discounting, fits three human data sets at least as well as the old rule and also fits data the old rule cannot (reward size effects).
numbers: Learning rate a fixed at 0.1; discount K fixed at 1.0; fits: R2=0.98, MSE=0.0008 (Friedman et al. probability learning, more than 1,000 trials over 3 days); R2=0.97, MSE=0.003 (second reward condition); R2=0.94, RMSE=0.007 (Busemeyer and Myung three-treatment task, 9 blocks of 50 trials, G fitted to 1.76). Discounting did not matter in the single-step tasks.
limits: This is the 2004 paper, NOT the 2006 Fu and Anderson credit-assignment paper (gap 8 stays open). Single-step choice tasks, so credit assignment for sequences is only described, not tested.
agent_relevance: The path from success counts to TD updates is a small change. For multi-step operator sequences, discounted credit with a=0.1 is the human-fit default to try against end-of-episode sharing.

source: Fu & Anderson (2006/2008) Solving the credit assignment problem: explicit and implicit learning of action sequences with probabilistic outcomes
finding: Search snippet only (full text blocked: HTTP 403 on DTIC, empty page on eScholarship). Abstract as reported: when explicit memory encoding dominates, people choose the better option faster on first than last choices; the reverse when implicit reinforcement learning dominates. Implicit reinforcement learning worked only with distinct external state information.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers. Journal version: Psychological Research 2008.
agent_relevance: Hint that credit assignment over sequences works only when each state is distinguishable. For the agent: keep operator statistics per distinct, visible context, not pooled.

source: Forouzandeh et al. (2025/2026) MACLA: Learning hierarchical procedural memory for LLM agents through Bayesian selection and contrastive refinement (AAMAS 2026)
finding: A frozen LLM plus an external memory of procedures, each with a Beta(alpha,beta) success posterior, chosen by an expected-utility score (relevance, expected reward, failure risk, entropy bonus). Removing the Bayesian selection gave the largest single loss among the components ablated on seen tasks.
numbers: ALFWorld, Llama-2-7B backbone: full 87.1-87.2 seen / 90.3 unseen; without Bayesian selection 79.4 / 81.2 (-7.8 / -9.1); without contrastive refinement 83.6 / 85.7; without meta-procedures 81.2 / 78.4; without ontology 82.8 / 84.1. Reuse rate 78% vs 62% without Bayesian selection; LLM calls per episode 6.2 vs 8.4. Four benchmarks average 78.1%. Memory built in 56 s. Example posterior Beta(10,3).
limits: The ablation replaces Bayesian selection with semantic-similarity ranking, NOT with random or fixed order. Procedures are skills, not reasoning operators. One value per cell, no CI in the text read. Utility mixes four terms, so success rate alone is not isolated. 7B backbone.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to the missing ablation (gap 1): learned success posteriors beat similarity-only choice by 7.8 to 9.1 points. Still not tested on reasoning operators, and no equal-token control.

source: Forouzandeh et al. (2025/2026) MACLA - cold start, capacity and pruning results
finding: The posterior mean per procedure rises from an optimistic start of 0.5 to about 0.79 as episodes accumulate. Procedures below 0.4 success are pruned. With about half the training data the system already reaches most of its final score.
numbers: 82% success using the first 1,425 trajectories (50% of data); 20% of data (570 trajectories) gives 45%. Pruned procedures mean posterior 0.42 vs retained 0.79. Capacity: 25 slots 68.3 seen / 64.1 unseen; 50 slots 83.1 / 85.6; 100 slots 87.2 / 90.3; 150 slots 86.4 / 88.7; 300 slots 87.1 / 90.1 (no gain). Posteriors converge above 0.75 within about 50 episodes.
limits: Learning curves are descriptive; no prior-strength sweep. Llama-2-7B backbone. Per-setting numbers, no CI.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: from a flat 0.5 start, tens of episodes per task family were needed. The agent should ship with informed priors or warm starts, and prune operators below about 0.4.

source: Life-sciences agents with Thompson sampling contextual bandits (arXiv 2512.03065, Dec 2025) - results and ablation
finding: A bandit chooses among generation strategy (direct vs chain of thought), tool and domain agent using user feedback. It beats uniform random, and removing parts lowers the score. This is the source behind earlier claim K12.
numbers: After 30 queries: strategy selection 23/30 (77%) vs random 15/30 (50%); tool selection 24/30 (80%) vs 14/30 (47%); domain routing 22/30 (73%) vs 15/30 (50%); average 76.7% vs 49.0%. Ablation (Table 7): without context features 58.3%; epsilon-greedy instead of Thompson 68.1%; without warm start 71.2%. Context dimension d=5 best (76.7%), d=3 71.2%, d=10 74.3%, d=20 69.8%. Queries to reach 70%: Thompson 18.3 (SD 4.2), epsilon-greedy 24.7 (SD 6.1), UCB 21.5 (SD 5.3).
limits: Only 30 queries per mode, no confidence intervals; the text calls the gain significant without a test. Reward is a binary user-satisfaction signal and random sits near 50% by design. The fixed-strategy baseline is defined but its numbers were not seen. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that learned strategy choice beats random in an LLM agent, but on a tiny sample. Warm start +5.5 points shows priors matter at cold start. Needs a rerun with 100+ items and CIs before use as proof.

source: Life-sciences Thompson sampling agents (arXiv 2512.03065) - cold start and non-stationarity design
finding: The paper proposes, but its results did not test, remedies for cold start (prior alpha0=2, beta0=1, a keyword warm start for the first 5 queries, transfer from similar deployments) and for drift (sliding window W=50, exponential forgetting factor 0.95).
numbers: Appendix hyperparameters: sliding window W=50, forgetting 0.95; generation temperature 0.7 for chain of thought, 0.5 for direct answers.
limits: Design suggestions, not measured results; no drift experiment found in the text read.
agent_relevance: Starting values for decay (0.95 per step, window 50) for gap 10, but untested for operators.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Think Fast and Slow: Step-level cognitive depth adaptation for LLM agents (CogRouter, arXiv 2602.12662)
finding: Four ACT-R-inspired cognitive levels from instinctive to strategic planning; a trained router picks the level at each step. Adaptive per-step choice beat every fixed level on both success and tokens. It is trained with SFT plus RL, not a scaffold.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B, ALFWorld: CogRouter 92.5% success with 1,739.4 tokens per trajectory; fixed level L1 76.5% with 357 tokens; fixed L4 86.5% with 4,641 tokens; FreeForm 81.5% with 4,069 tokens. Abstract headline: 82.3% success, GPT-4o +40.3, o3 +18.3, GRPO +14.0, with 62% fewer tokens (GRPO 4,367 tokens vs 1,641). ScienceWorld 72.0% for the best confidence metric.
limits: Learned policy by gradient training, not utility counts. The 82.3% headline and the 92.5% ALFWorld figure come from different tables or settings and were not reconciled. Compares to fixed levels (the fixed-order control missing elsewhere) but not to random level choice in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Best evidence so far that picking reasoning depth per step beats any fixed choice at lower token cost (gap 1, partial). A counts-based selector is the training-free analogue to test.

source: Yang et al. (2026) CogRouter - ablation on credit assignment and cold start (arXiv 2602.12662)
finding: Step-level credit assignment (confidence-reweighted advantage, successful trajectories only) beat uniform trajectory-level credit. Without a balanced cold start, the router collapsed to one level.
numbers: ALFWorld: average log-probability confidence 92.5%; max-prob variant 89.0%; entropy 79.0%; min-prob 81.5%. Without cold start 86.0% (2,496 tokens, 0.3% L1); initialised from GPT-4o's chosen levels 87.5% (2,872 tokens, 92.1% L3); reweighting failed trajectories too 83.0% (1,376 tokens, collapse to L1 83.1%). GiGPO also collapses to L4 thinking.
limits: Row alignment in the extracted table is partly garbled; only numbers stated in the prose were used. Gradient RL, not a counts rule.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: step-level credit mattered, and punishing failures pushed the router to the cheapest operator. Warning that failure penalties can cause collapse, so cost and success must be balanced.

source: Barkan, Black & Sourbut (2025) Do large language models know what they are capable of? (arXiv 2512.24661)
finding: All tested LLMs overestimate their own chance of success before attempting a task. Discrimination between solvable and unsolvable tasks is above chance for most. After failures in context, some models (Claude Sonnet) learn to decline; GPT-4.1 hardly changes. Their accept/decline decisions are close to rational given their stated probabilities, so the problem is the estimate.
numbers: Experiment 2: 512 sequences of 9 contracts, win 1 dollar / lose 1 dollar, 50% of contracts solvable. Sonnet 3.5 reached the ideal 50% acceptance by contract 5; GPT-4.1 predicted success showed almost no change. All LLMs stay above 0.5 predicted success despite failing 50%. Experiment 3 (multi-step tasks): Sonnet models become more overconfident as they progress; only GPT-4o becomes substantially less so; reasoning models no better.
limits: Self-estimates of success on coding tasks, not operator success. Exact AUROC and overconfidence values are in figures and were not extracted. An earlier version was accepted at NeurIPS 2025.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: asking the model to rate an operator's chance is biased upward and stays so after failures. Keep success counts in the scaffold; do not ask the model.

source: Kaddour et al. (2026) Agentic uncertainty reveals agentic overconfidence (arXiv 2602.06948, ICLR 2026)
finding: Coding agents asked for their success probability before, during and after a task are overconfident everywhere. Asking before the run, with less information, discriminated about as well or better than reviewing the finished patch. Asking the agent to find bugs cut overconfidence.
numbers: 100 SWE-bench Pro tasks; base success GPT-5.2-Codex 35%, Gemini 3 Pro 22%, Claude Opus 4.5 27%. Post-execution predicted success 73% (GPT), 77% (Gemini), 61% (Claude). Gemini pre-execution mean estimate 99%. 62% of predictions on failing tasks were 0.7 or higher; only 11% of passing tasks predicted below 0.3 (5.5x asymmetry). Adversarial review lowered the overconfident-failure rate from 72% to 45%. Mid-run: confidence fell with progress for 71% of GPT and 97% of Claude runs.
limits: N=100 tasks, wide CIs, AUROC differences often not significant. One benchmark, three models.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: current confirmation that self-reported success is inflated (up to 77% vs 22%). Count-based operator success avoids this. Adversarial framing is a cheap fix if a self-estimate is unavoidable.

source: Taberner-Miller (2026) ParetoBandit: budget-paced adaptive routing for non-stationary LLM serving (arXiv 2604.00136)
finding: A contextual-bandit LLM router with geometric forgetting of old statistics tracks silent quality drops and price changes, and brings in a new model within 142 steps. Budget control came from a separate pacer, not from the forgetting.
numbers: 1,824 prompts, 3 models, 20 seeds, 95% bootstrap CI. Forgetting factor 0.997. Silent regression of one model to reward 0.75 (18% below normal): its share fell from 71% to 50% in the bad phase; after recovery its share rose to 54% and reward recovered to 0.8630 [0.8572, 0.8684] vs 0.8850 before (ratio 0.975). Cost within 0.4% of budget. Cold-started model adopted in all 80 trials within 142 steps; a bad model was rejected in every seed.
limits: Simulated drift on replayed benchmark data; rewards are judge scores; arms are models, not reasoning operators. The 18% degradation was within the recovery envelope; larger drops may need longer horizons (Appendix G). Author states no other LLM router uses discounting or windows.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: decayed counts (gamma 0.997 per step in a stream of thousands) recover from silent operator failure, with forced re-exploration when counts go stale. Fits utility rules that already decay old experience.

source: Feng et al. (2026) Break it down, pass it on: cross-task skill transfer in LLM agents (arXiv 2608.20274v2) - verified and extended
finding: The arXiv id is real (v2, 16 Oct 2026). Skills learnt from whole tasks transfer badly and can hurt; skills learnt per subtask help on average. Text skills transfer better than code skills. Replaying subtask skills into the task-level agent confirmed the effect travels with the skills.
numbers: Eleven models; AppWorld, OfficeBench, KramaBench. Task-level skills lowered average success by 1.2 points (text) and 4.1 (code); subtask-level raised it by 1.9 (text) and 0.5 (code). Code skills lost 1.4 points on KramaBench. Worst case: GPT-OSS-120B on AppWorld fell from 27.3% to 1.0% with task-level code skills; in 69% of those tasks the agent stopped within two steps. Utility bins 14.0% to 24.5% (task-level), 22.8% to 31.0% (subtask-level), Spearman 0.98 and 0.95. Task-level skills help mainly where the no-memory baseline is very low.
limits: The utility score is text-similarity based (specificity times abstractness), not observed success. Gains of 0.5 to 1.9 points are small. CIs are 95% task-bootstrap.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: sharing across tasks is not free: whole-task rules harmed. Share operator statistics at a coarse subtask level and measure harm against a no-memory control. Outcome-based sharing is still untested.

source: Lim et al. (2025) TextBandit: evaluating probabilistic reasoning in LLMs through language-only decision tasks (arXiv 2510.13878)
finding: With only text feedback ('you earned a token'), most small open LLMs did worse than classical bandit rules, but Qwen3-4B beat them all.
numbers: 500 independent runs of 25 iterations, 2 to 5 arms, best arm win rate 65%. Best-arm selection: Qwen3-4B 89.2%; Qwen3-8B 37.5%; Llama-3.1-8B 31.6%; Phi-2 25.4%; Thompson sampling 51.1%; UCB 47.6%; epsilon-greedy 38.1%; random 31.8%.
limits: Only four small open models, short horizon (25 steps); the Qwen3-4B result is not explained or replicated. Single-shot completions with history in the prompt.
agent_relevance: Another sign that LLM-chosen arms are unreliable; Thompson sampling is the best simple baseline here (51.1% vs random 31.8% in 25 steps).

source: Zhang, Wang, Chen, Mansur & Sarhangian (2025/2026) Comparing exploration-exploitation strategies of LLMs and humans (arXiv 2505.09901v3)
finding: Fits an inverse-temperature (random exploration) plus uncertainty-bonus (directed exploration) choice model to humans, LLMs and bandit algorithms. Plain LLMs show more random and less directed exploration; chain of thought shifts them toward the human mix. In a changing (non-stationary) task LLMs fail at directed exploration, even where regret is similar.
numbers: Two canonical bandit experiments, stationary and non-stationary; thinking models and chain-of-thought prompts compared with humans. Specific coefficient values were not extracted.
limits: Choice-model fits, not task accuracy. Numerical results not recorded.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 10: a softmax temperature is the random-exploration knob; LLMs left alone have too much of it and too little directed exploration, so the scaffold should own both temperature and uncertainty bonus.

source: Sun, Wang, Yang et al. (2025) Large language model-enhanced multi-armed bandits (arXiv 2502.01118)
finding: A classical Thompson sampling frame where the LLM only predicts rewards, with the LLM temperature decayed over time to move from exploration to exploitation. Reported to beat direct LLM arm selection on synthetic and text-dataset bandits.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read: a decaying temperature schedule is said to beat a fixed temperature (Sec 5.1); temperature 0 for the regression-oracle variant. No regret numbers extracted.
limits: Only abstract-level claims recorded. The temperature is the LLM sampling temperature, not an ACT-R utility noise. Arms are text items, not reasoning operators.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: supports decaying the softmax temperature over time rather than a constant 0.5. The sweep still has to be run on operators.
